case_name: Durham Children's Aid Society v. R.B.
text:
WHITBY
COURT
FILE NO.:

871/02

DATE:

January 3, 2006

ONTARIO

SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE

FAMILY COURT

B E T W E E N:

)

)

The Durham
Children’s Aid Society

))

Applicant

)

Farrah Manji
counsel for the Applicant

- and -

)

R… B…

))

)

)

)

Robert Sochor,
counsel for the respondent

Joanne Ferguson,
counsel for the child A.B.

Respondents

HEARD:  April
20, 21, 22, 2005 June  6, 9, 10, 2005 Oct. 11, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 24, 25,
26, 27, 28, 2005
Nov. 9,
2005

ROGERS
J.

RULING

[
1
]

The Children’s Aid
Society of the Region of Durham has applied to the court to have a finding that
A… B… is a child in need of protection and ought to be made a crown ward. The
request is there be an order for “no access” so that the child might be
adopted. Her mother, R… B…, resists these requests.  She asks that the child
not be found in need of protection. Where A…B… to be found to be a child in
need of protection, Ms R…B… requests that A…B… be placed with her and her
sister, C… B…, jointly or with C… B… such that she could reside with her sister
and A…B…. Ms R… B… would agree to supervision of the placement by a children’s
aid society.

[
2
]

This trial originally
included a claim about A…B…’s older brother, O…B…. A consent was reached
regarding O…B…. He is now a crown ward and his mother has access. This consent
is based on an acknowledgement by all that O…B… requires special assistance
that Ms R… B… cannot provide.

[
3
]

This trial took place
more than three years after A…B… was apprehended at four month’s of age. Such
an inordinate delay has had consequences for all concerned, especially A…B….

[
4
]

There was a last minute
change in the plan of the mother to include her sister, Ms C… B…, as a joint
placement. Although the respondent mother’s plan always involved her and A…B…
residing at her sister’s home with help from her sister, the formal joint plan
came during the trial. The alternate plan that A…B…’s aunt, Ms C… B…, be
considered as a placement on her own was canvassed by the court during
testimony by Ms C… B…. This alternate plan was adopted by the respondent
mother. Each of these plans seemed similar to the mother in that she would be
living with her daughter at her sister’s home and sharing responsibility for
the care of A…B… with her sister. That was how she envisioned this family
constellation functioning. However, each articulated plan is different to the
court in that R… B… has descending degrees of control over the decisions about
A…B…. A placement solely with R… B… means she makes the decisions alone. Next,
a placement with the two sisters means they jointly decide. Finally, a
placement with C… B… gives her alone ultimate control.

Ms R… B… ’s Background

[
5
]

R… B… was one of nine
children. Her father committed suicide when she was yet unborn. The
difficulties experienced by the family of origin after her father’s death led
to R… B… being in foster care for about five years from about the age of five
to ten. She was in foster care with her sister C…B… who is two years older. Both
women speak of the coldness of the foster family where there were already
twelve children before they arrived. They were picked on, particularly the
younger child, R… B…. C…B… testified that the treatment of her younger sister
was particularly hurtful and she suffered considerably.

[
6
]

The respondent mother, Ms
R… B…, struggled all through her formative years with school. She never
achieved more than approximately grade three level in reading while in school.
As noted above, she returned to her mother’s home at about ten years of age and
later left at about sixteen. She had a long-standing relationship with a man in

Toronto
with whom she had a child, N…, born
in1980. Upon their separation, N… resided with her mother at times, her father
at times and was also in care. Her qualms about living with her mother were
mostly because of her mother’s boyfriend, M… C…. Since her mid teens, N… has
been on her own. She has a son and resides in western
Canada
.

[
7
]

Some time after R… B…
separated from N.’s father, she went to live in
Calgary
.
There she formed a relationship with M… C… with whom she had a child, O…B…,
born December 1, 1994. Ms R… B… and O…B… moved back and forth between
Calgary
and
British
Columbia
with M… C… coming in
and out of their lives. In 1999 M… C… assaulted Ms R… B… and was charged with
assault. He departed for
Ontario
with O…B… residing with Ms R… B….

Ms R… B… ’s Achievements

[
8
]

While in
British Columbia
, Ms R… B… took upgrading courses. She improved her
reading skills to about grade seven or eight. During the trial it was obvious
that she struggles to read, particularly difficult documents. But she has
attained a level sufficient to maintain employment and get by in a literate
world.

[
9
]

Ms R… B…, as observed
in the trial, does have difficulty expressing herself verbally, but she is not
lacking analytical skills. She clearly thinks through difficulties and
considers them. During testimony she was asked some complicated questions; she
paused, thought them through and tried to convey her conclusions. Her language
skills clearly impede her ability to communicate some considered ideas. Her
cognitive testing showed a borderline ability but this testing was done at an
enormously stressful time in her life. The testing itself speculated that she
did not perform at her true capacity. She is not simple or unthinking. Over her
lifetime her behaviour has been foolish or worse at times, but she can reason
through alternatives and analyse options. While it seems she has often made bad
decisions, she is capable of working through to better ones.

[
10
]

Ms R… B… now has her
two jobs and her home is with her sister. She hopes to move into full time work
at the nursing home and would quit at Tim Horton’s if that happened. She has
planned quite impressively for activities and day care for A…B…. She is
prepared to use whatever services are needed for A…B….

Involvement with Child Protection Authorities

[
11
]

In spite of her efforts
to enhance her literacy and work skills, R… B… was poorly equipped to deal with
poverty and single parenthood. Her connection with M… C… was unfortunate in
that his judgment was poor and her family truly abhorred him. The combination
of these factors led Ms R… B… to involvements with child protection
authorities.

[
12
]

Ms R… B… was involved
with the
British Columbia
child protection authorities in May 2000.
Their precise concerns were not in evidence before the court because no one
from that agency testified. However, it is clear that they visited Ms R… B… the
day before she left for
Ontario
. She testified that she was not fleeing
their intervention but going to
Niagara
Falls,
Ontario
to visit with her son’s paternal
grandparents and M… C…, O.B.’s father. She insists she told them that. M… C…
had purchased a ticket for Ms R… B… and O…B…. C… B… testified that R… B… complained
it was a one-way ticket when it was supposed to be a return ticket. In any
event, the
British Columbia
authorities issued a
Canada
wide alert for her and O…B….  When the child welfare
authorities from Niagara came to speak with R… B… she made one of her many bad
decisions and went out the other door with O…B…. She made her way to
Montreal
where she had family. The child protection agency in
Montreal
became aware of her presence and apprehended O…B….

[
13
]

In January 2001 R… B…
and her brother V…B… had an altercation. Both had been drinking. Her brother
emerged from this fight somewhat the worse for it with a broken nose. Ms R… B…
was charged with attempted murder. In what appears to be post charge diversion,
Ms R… B… entered a treatment facility for substance abuse called Freedom House.
In her testimony it seemed Ms R… B… picked up quite a number of helpful ideas
from her time there. Ultimately her charge was reduced to aggravated assault
and she received a conditional sentence. During her time at Freedom House she
had passes to have daytime access with O…B….

[
14
]

The use of alcohol and
drugs had been a familiar theme in R… B…’s life. There were also at least two
periods when she had resorted to prostitution for money. From her testimony it
was clear that she learned much at Freedom House about why dependence on
substances was causing her difficulty and how her poor self-esteem led her to
an inappropriate lifestyle.

[
15
]

During all of this time
O…B… was in care. Originally the serious issue was the risk of flight but the
involvement in the criminal justice system took Ms R… B… out of a care giving
role. But other concerns emerged soon after the apprehension. O…B… was an
extremely difficult child to manage. His behaviour was so extreme that the
school would not keep him. The
Montreal
child protection authorities arranged,
with some considerable difficulty, to have him treated as a day patient at the
Montreal Jewish General Hospital.   His mother was included in this process.
The hospital was not very welcoming to Ms R… B… but the social worker advocated
for her and she did participate. There was a considerable argument about the
use of the drug, Ritalin, for O…B… who by this time was diagnosed with
Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder. Ms R… B… opposed the use but it was
administered anyway. Soon it became clear that O…B… had serious side effects
and it was discontinued. O…B… otherwise made great gains in this program.

[
16
]

The child protection
authorities in
Quebec
were also concerned with Ms R… B…’s
minimizing of O.B.’s difficulties. She insisted that his behaviour problems
were because he had been taken from her. The child protection authorities began
to work intensively with Ms R… B…. Her main social worker was Mr. Kastanek. He
was a very experienced worker with an open mind. This court was very impressed
with his fairness, diligence in assisting Ms R… B… and his wisdom about
people.  He formed a circle of helpers for Ms R… B… to take her through her
difficulties but also to help her understand O…B… and prepare to parent him.
The circle included several professionals but also at times family and
community people such as friends from Ms R… B…’s church. The meetings were
frequent and helpful. Mr. Kastanek also helped Ms R… B… with many of her other
life difficulties, advocating for her when needed. By such intensive and
supportive initiatives, Mr. Kastanek and his agency was able to overcome her
very suspicious approach to the authorities and begin the journey of teaching
her how to parent O…B…. The child was returned to her care in 2002. When A…B…
was born, there was no intervention by the
Quebec

authorities.

[
17
]

Mr Kastanek remained
involved and became concerned when Mr M…C… appeared, presumably to visit O…B….
All of the child protection authorities had Mr. M…C…’s criminal record
available to them. He has twenty-four findings of guilt from 1986 through to
2000. Some of the findings stem from the same event. They include property
crimes, events involving substance abuse, failure to obey court orders and
assaultive behaviour. The evidence is not clear as to whether he ever served
time in the federal penitentiary system. While not one of the country’s worst
criminals by any account, Mr M…C… was a persistent and unreformed presence in
the criminal courts. As well, R… B…’s family, particularly C…B…, intensely
disliked him.  Regrettably, some difficulty between R… B…’s uncle and nephew
and Mr. M…C… caused an event where the two family members assaulted Mr. M…C…. Ms
R… B… was elsewhere with the children but the assault took place in her
apartment. Mr. M…C… was injured and stayed in Ms R… B…’s apartment. She left
the children with a friend and tended to Mr. M…C…. Mr. Kastanek was concerned
that she got her priorities wrong and should have tended to the children, not
Mr. M…C….

[
18
]

By this time, although
Mr. Kastanek was concerned, there was a plan for Ms R…B… and the children to
move to
Ontario
in a planned fashion so that services for
them and a school for O…B… could be organized. At this time Mr. Kasternac went
on sabbatical and a new worker took over. Ms R… B… purchased a van so she and
the children could move. She only had a learner’s permit to drive and needed a
driver. Unfortunately, M… C… was the driver. The search for a new home took
them to C… B…’s in
Toronto
where predictably C… B… told the
respondent that she and the children could stay, but not Mr. M…C….
Unfortunately, R… B… did not listen to her sister. She ended up in
Oshawa
considering relocation to that area. She stayed at
the YWCA. There she told the staff she was involved with the child protection
authorities and gave them a phone number for the authorities in
Montreal
. The staff was somewhat concerned about O.B.’s
behaviour. They were also unsure as to Ms R… B…’s supplies for A…B…, not
knowing, of course, that many of her possessions were left at C… B…’s. They
called the Durham Children’s Aid Society, hereinafter called the Durham CAS.

[
19
]

The Durham CAS attended
at the shelter. The concerns raised were about O…B…'s behaviour, the presence
of a man called Dave who was really M… C…, seemingly poor of care of A…B…, a
cigarette burn on A…B… and A…B…’s need for medication for a kidney problem.

[
20
]

Unfortunately at the
time of an apprehension, the facts are not well known because of the urgency of
the situation. No doubt O…B…'s behaviour was difficult. The purpose of a
planned move was to provide services for him. A…B… did have a kidney problem
then but the evidence at trial did not show she was improperly or inadequately
medicated. There was a good explanation for the burn as Mr M…C… had flicked a
cigarette out of the car window and it had blown back in, landing on A…B….
There was no evidence of intent. However, again, Ms R…B…’s connection to Mr.
M…C… caused great concern. The foolishness of being with him, let alone
deceiving all about him caused great concern about her ability to priorize her
children over a violent man. His surliness, his uncooperative manner and his
seemingly threatening presence caused even greater concerns as workers felt Ms
R…B… could not or would not work with them when he was around. The apprehension
was understandable. Unfortunately, an immediate return of Ms R…B… and the
children to
Quebec
where there was already much work done
under the supervision order would have served all better. She then could have
restarted the move to
Ontario
with help from the
Quebec
authorities with whom she had a working relationship.
The trust that the
Quebec
agency had built with Ms R…B… was the best
hope that she could plan appropriately for her children and also understand the
destructive role Mr. M…C… played in her life.

[
21
]

After the apprehension Ms
R…B… lingered around the
Oshawa
area but she had to confront the fact that
she ought to have been residing in
Quebec
in accordance
with her conditional sentence. Mr. Kasternac had explained to her that she
could not just leave
Quebec
without transferring the supervision of
her sentence. She had not begun that process when she went to
Ontario
to seek a new location but ended up with the children
being apprehended. She had to return to
Quebec

and did so in October 2002. She visited the children infrequently during this
time. By April 2003 she was able to leave
Quebec
.
She came briefly to
Oshawa
but quickly relocated to
Kitchener
where she lived with Mr. and Mrs. C… senior. Then
with M… C…’s financial help she got her own apartment. She set about getting
employment often working two jobs. She took two parenting courses, one of which
was about children with ADHD. She attended for many drug and urine screens. She
attended for her monthly visit with the children often having to leave about
5:30 am
.

[
22
]

While Ms R…B… was
beginning to organize her life, M… C… was still impeding her progress. There is
no doubt there were many times when Mr. M…C… was helpful. Ms R…B… was very poor
and he helped out financially. His parents provided her with a home and
support. Ms R…B… felt Mr. M…C… was trying to support her in her quest to have
O…B… returned because it was the only way he could maintain a relationship with
his son. Unfortunately the police were called to Ms R…B…’s home two times when
Mr. M…C… was drunk. Once Ms R… B… was intoxicated as well.

[
23
]

In November 2004 Ms
R…B… finally came to terms with the destructive influence of Mr. M…C…. She
moved to her sister’s home. C…B… testified that she has not seen her abusing
alcohol. M… C… is not allowed in C… B…’s home and has not been in Ms R…B…’s
life. R… B… has her two jobs. She keeps house along with her sister. There was
a home study of this arrangement that was positive.

A Finding that A…B… is in Need of Protection

[
24
]

The court is asked to
make a finding pursuant to section 37(2)(b)(ii) or 37(2)(e).

37(2) A child is in need of protection where,

(a)

the child has suffered
physical harm, inflicted by the person having charge of the child or caused by
or resulting from that person’s,

(i)  failure to adequately care for, providing for,
supervising or protecting the     child.

(ii)  pattern of neglect in caring for, providing for,
supervising or protecting the child.

(e)  the child requires medical treatment to cure,
prevent or alleviate physical harm    or suffering and the child’s parent or
the person having charge of the child does not provide, or refuses or is
unavailable or unable to consent to, the treatment.

[
25
]

It is most unusual that
there would not have been a “finding” before this date. This child has been in
care since July 2002. However, the finding that a child is in need of
protection is not based on the facts as they exist today. The consideration is
of facts from the time of the apprehension forward.

[
26
]

The allegations to
substantiate a finding pursuant to section 37(2)(e) have not been proven. The
cigarette burn was an accident. The tissue damage was small and Ms R…B…’s care
for it was not unreasonable. Neglect in administering or failing to administer
the medication for A…B…’s kidney condition has not been proven.

[
27
]

The grounds in section
37(2)(b)(ii) are more concerning. Ms R…B… has repeatedly exhibited poor
judgment in her parenting such that she has not been reliably able to care for,
provide for, supervise or protect her children. While the court acknowledges
that her poverty and childhood have contributed substantially to her
difficulties, she has repeatedly made bad choices that hurt her children,
particularly O…B…. Whether or not she ran from the
British Columbia
authorities, she did not provide a clear
understanding of her intentions to them. She ran from the authorities in
Niagara. She got herself involved with the criminal justice system in
Quebec
to such an extent that she could not be available for
O…B…. Then Mr. M…C… arrived and she priorized him over the children.

[
28
]

The pattern re emerges
in
Ontario
in this case. She planned to move to
Ontario
but does not communicate that well to the
Quebec
authorities. She did not avail herself of their
assistance in seeking a new location. She chose Mr. M…C… to help her move. She
and the children could have stayed with her sister, C…B… but she chose to leave
that safe place because C…B… cannot tolerate Mr. M…C…. While she could not have
foreseen the fact of the apprehension, she did not deal with the criminal
justice system personnel to transfer the serving of her conditional sentence
before she went looking for a residence in
Ontario
.
It should have been obvious that all of these considerations had to be dealt
with so that the move would be smooth.  Ms R…B… also should have known that the

Quebec
child welfare authorities,
Quebec

probation and certainly her sister would not approve of Mr. M…C…’s presence.
While she no doubt needed support to move, she looked for it in the wrong
person and ignored all the more appropriate helpers.

[
29
]

Counsel for the CAS of
Durham and the Children’s Lawyer were critical of Ms R…B… settling in
Kitchener
after she was able to leave
Quebec
.
This court understands the need to have a support system but C… B… would have
been a better choice. Again, Ms R…B… turned to Mr. M…C…. While it is true that
he and his parents had and did help her, it ought to have been obvious to Ms
R…B… then, if not sooner, that her connection to Mr. M…C… brought trouble. This
she could little afford for herself let alone her children. As might be
expected, there were police occurrences at that home and she clearly drank to
intoxication at least once when Mr. M…C… was at her home. While she did many
good things in
Kitchener
, her involvement with Mr. M…C… at whatever
level was not helping her establish herself and make a home for the children.
She should never have thought that she could expect to have them returned to
her if she was maintaining a relationship with Mr. M…C… and she ought to have
gone further than that and seen how he impeded her progress in improving her
own life. It is noteworthy that every time Ms R…B… seemed to be leaving some
child protection authorities and causing anxiety about her departure, Mr. M…C…
was involved; the departure from
British
Columbia
on the ticket he
provided, the departure from his parent’s home in
Niagara

and the unplanned, undisclosed journey to
Ontario

with M… C… as driver and potential cohabitant.

[
30
]

The old problem of
resorting to alcohol surfaced in
Kitchener
. Ms R…B… did a great many screens that
were clean. Although there were gaps in the provision of screens, her evidence
that she sometimes skipped screens because of the pressure of work is
plausible. However, when M… C… was around at her home, she drank on at least
one occasion to the point of intoxication.

[
31
]

This pattern of poor
decisions continued until she realized the M… C… connection was damaging and
she moved to C… B…’s home.

[
32
]

The court finds that
A…B… is in need of protection pursuant to section 37 (2)(b)(ii).

Disposition

[
33
]

The task of the court
in making a disposition for a child is set out in section 57. A number of steps
have to be taken in the process of reaching a decision.

a)   Section 57(1) Orders Available

[
34
]

In considering the
options available all parties agreed that the time for a society wardship order
has long passed. The only orders possible are a supervision order or crown
wardship with or without access.

b)   Section 57 (2): Duty to Inquire

[
35
]

The court in deciding
disposition is to inquire as to the efforts made by the society or any other
agency or person to assist the child. In this case the Durham Children’s Aid
Society made no efforts to assist the child before intervention. The
Quebec
authorities had worked intensively with R… B… because
of O…B… and had decided no intervention was necessary for A…B…. There was still
a supervision order for O…B… but the worker supported Ms R…B…’s plan to move to

Ontario
if it was a planned move with appropriate
supports built in.

c) Section 57 (3): Less Disruptive Alternative

[
36
]

This section reads as
follows:

(57(3)  The
court shall not make an order removing the child from the care of the person
who had charge of him or her immediately before intervention under this Part
unless the court is satisfied that alternatives that are less disruptive to the
child, including non-residential services and the assistance referred to in
subsection (2), would be inadequate to protect the child.

This section causes the court to
examine alternatives that are less disruptive to the child than removal from
the family. The extraordinary delay in this case and the lack of efforts as
noted in section 57(2) have turned this section on its head. A…B… was so young
when she was removed from her mother and she has been in the foster home so
long that the disruption would be in removing her from the foster family.

d) Section 57 (4): Plans of the Biological Family

[
37
]

There have been several
plans put forth by the biological family. The maternal grandparents have twice
asked for consideration and withdrawn. C… B… noted that her stepfather is
elderly and unwell. Mr. M…C…’s family came forward at one point but never
followed through. R… B… notes that not long after their intended planning, Mr.
M…C… senior took ill and died. C… B… previously put forth a plan to care for
both the children but withdrew this plan upon reflection. She testified that
she had to take into consideration that O…B… had very high needs. At that time
she was not confident that her sister, R…B…, would pull through her
difficulties. Then she was terminated from her job and was worried about her
finances. Now she is prepared to plan for A…B…, with or without R… B…’s help.
She visited with A…B… regularly and showed a good understanding of and respect
for the child’s needs. She has retrained, has a job she feels confident about
and feels R… B… will succeed in overcoming her past and be able to help parent
A…B…. If R… B… fails, C… B… is prepared to go it alone and be A…B…’s mother.

[
38
]

The plan to place A…B…
solely with her aunt emerged during C… B…’s evidence. Section 57 (4) requires
the court to consider a placement in the community with a relative or friend
before turning to the alternative of crown wardship.

[
39
]

In her evidence in
chief C… B… committed to helping her sister for up to a year and a half. She
was completely confident that her sister could take over care of A…B… fully by
then. In cross examination about her earlier withdrawal of a plan, it became
apparent the difficulties of parenting O…B… figured significantly in her
decision to withdraw her plan to care for the two children earlier. However,
for the court to consider a community placement it meant that stability of such
a placement was at issue. There could not be a breakdown of such a placement
because A…B… needs a permanent plan. Even though C… B… is persuaded that R… B…
has turned her life around, the court would want assurance of a stable
placement if Ms R… B… fails. That would come from a commitment to permanent
planning by C… B…. The court had to know if her aunt would care for A…B… if her
mother failed as an appropriate caregiver. This evidence was vital to the
process in section 57(4). C… B… understood the continuity of care issue, if not
the legal issue in section 57 (4) and, upon a break for reflection, committed
to this child. The court asked her to think on this commitment over a ten-day
break in the trial and to withdraw such a commitment by the time of
submissions. She did not withdraw. R… B… adopted this plan with enthusiasm.

[
40
]

The court has also had
the advantage of a parenting capacity assessment done by Dr. Graham Berman.
This gentleman is a psychiatrist with many, many years of experience in this
field. Dr. Berman had available to him a report by Ms Beaudoin done in
Quebec
for the court there. There was psychological testing
done in this report. Although in Ontario the qualifications of Ms Beaudoin
would not be sufficient for admission to the Ontario Board of Examiners in Psychology
as a psychologist, she was qualified in Quebec to perform the work done and was
accepted as an expert in this court for the work in the report. Dr. Berman
testified that, although she would not qualify as a psychologist in
Ontario
, he had a lot of respect for the organization she
worked for. He felt the testing underestimated Ms R…B…’s ability but believed
that this did not suggest the testing was not valid but rather the
circumstances under which the testing occurred were particularly difficult for Ms
R…B…. This was a time of high stress for Ms R…B… just after O…B… was
apprehended.

[
41
]

Dr. Berman had less
than complete evidence about the Durham CAS’ concerns and Ms R…B…’s history.
However, after cross examination, he still felt that Ms R…B… had the capacity
to parent A…B… and that it was unfortunate that the child had been removed from
her mother for so long. Dr. Berman was also concerned about A…B…’s behaviour
before access as noted by the foster mother. The extremes of seeming resistance
to access did not fit with the child Dr. Berman saw in the observation. He felt
the child was very competent emotionally and in other areas of development. He
felt a child with a good secure attachment to the primary parent, the foster
mother, would not show the stated degree of regression in going to some safe
and regular activity. He said there was nothing going on in the access that
would induce this level of anxiety.  He wondered if anxiety about the case in
the foster home had been unconsciously transferred onto A…B….

[
42
]

Dr. Berman quite
clearly highlighted the difficulty A…B… would have in leaving her foster
family. He noted that, subject to some unknown difficulties in the foster home
shown in the excessive reaction of A…B… to the access, he was prepared to
assume A…B… had a secure attachment to the foster mother and had developed the
ability to attach to people. As he saw Ms R…B… as having the ability to parent
A…B…, the attachment could form.

[
43
]

The court has had the
opportunity to hear and see the mother and aunt of A…B…. Both these women have
come a long way from their difficult childhoods. Ms R… B… has also struggled
with reading and communication challenges.  Both women impressed the court as
thoughtful and careful. Ms R… B… would become confused with open-ended questions
but would struggle to answer. Both women stated their goals in life clearly.
Both women are sensitive to the needs of others and fair in considering such.
They are tuned into the dilemma facing A…B…’s foster parents and brothers if
she leaves. And both women are acutely aware of how hard it would be for A…B…
to lose her foster family.

[
44
]

Based on the evidence
from other witnesses and the documents filed, on the testimony of the mother
and aunt, on their demeanor and on the care they took to present their
evidence, the court finds that R…B… and C… B… together have the necessary
skills to care for A…B…. Further, the court finds that C… B… has the
understanding of the situation that she would recognize help was needed and
advocate for this little family to get the service needed. It remains to be
seen if R… B… has developed the determination to advocate for herself and A…B….

[
45
]

The court is not
satisfied that there has been sufficient duration to the lifestyle changes R…
B… has demonstrated. Nor does she presently have the skills to acquire help if
needed. She still lacks confidence and her difficulties putting her thoughts
into words causes her frustration and limits her effectiveness. She may develop
these skills but they are sorely needed now and are absent. As well the court
cannot be confident that R… B… has been able to improve sufficiently on her
past history of very bad decision making. She has made good decisions about her
work habits, her residence and her associates over the past year but this is not
enough assurance of success when seen against the backdrop of her past
mistakes. Only time will tell if she can continue on her new path. For this
reason the court cannot place A…B… with her alone.

[
46
]

It is also for this
reason that the court feels any placement with the B… sisters must provide C…
B… with the power to control A…B…’s life. It is clear that C… B… will consult
and work with R… B…. She is not looking to usurp his sister’s role in A…B…’s
life. She is not fulfilling a personal need. Further, the court is satisfied
from C… B…’s evidence that she has the fortitude and the determination to take
charge if necessary and act singularly for A…B…’s best interest. C… B… clearly
loves her sister and is proud of her gains, but she knows that A…B… is the priority.
Given C… B…’s commitment to permanent care for A…B…, the court is satisfied
that a placement with C… B…, with or without R… B…, is a good plan.

e)  Best Interests

[
47
]

The court must then
turn to Section 57 (1) which directs the court to make one of the permitted
orders in the child’s best interests. The criteria for best interests of a
child are found in section 37 (3) which reads as follows:

37(3) Where a
person is directed in this Part to make an order or determination in the best
interests of a child, the person shall take into consideration those of the
following circumstances of the case that he or she considers relevant:

1.    The child’s physical, mental and emotional
needs, and the appropriate care or treatment to meet those needs.

2.     The child’s physical, mental and emotional
level of development.

3.     The child’s cultural background.

4.     The religious faith, if any, in which the child
is being raised.

5.     The importance for the child’s development of a
positive relationship with a parent and a secure place as a member of a family.

6.     The child’s relationships by blood or through
an adoption order.

7.    The importance of continuity of the child’s care
and the possible effect on the child of disruption of that continuity.

8.    The merits of a plan for the child’s care
proposed by a society, including a proposal that the child be placed for
adoption or adopted, compared with the merits of the child remaining with or
returning to a parent.

9.

The child’s views and
wishes, if they can be reasonably ascertained.

10.

The effects on the
child of delay in the disposition of the case.

11.

The risk that the child
may suffer harm through being removed from, kept away from, returned to or
allowed to remain in the care of a parent.

12.

The degree of risk, if
any, that justified the finding that the child is in need of protection,

13.

Any other relevant
circumstance.

[
48
]

Criteria one of the
best interest sections is less significant in A.B.’s case than that of her
brother, O…B…. A…B… is a well-developed child in all aspects. She is
functioning well and has no special needs.  The critical need would be for the
proper assistance for A…B… and R…B… and C… B… if she is removed from the foster
home. Dr. Berman spoke of the need for on-site therapeutic assistance if this
happened as A…B… would be mourning the loss of her foster family.

[
49
]

A…B…’s physical,
emotional and emotional level of development as addressed in criteria two of
section 37 (3) are age appropriate and do not present any special challenges.

[
50
]

There has been no
evidence relating to the child’s cultural and religious background as in
criteria three and four.

[
51
]

Criteria five speaks to
the child’s development of a positive relationship with a parent and her
development as a secure member of a family. There is no doubt that A…B… is a
loved and happy member of the foster family and that she has an attachment with
her foster mother. However, she has exhibited such extreme reactions prior to
the stepped up access visits that Dr. Berman expressed some concern as to
possible difficulties in the foster family.  He felt the visits themselves
could not account for such a reaction. He also felt that the child demonstrated
such competence that such a presentation did not fit this child. Dr. Berman
worried that there was something in the foster home that was causing such an
unusual reaction. He wondered if the anxieties of the foster family were being
transferred to A…B….

[
52
]

The respondent mother
and C… B… are the child’s blood relatives and part of a large and diverse family
group. This family has suffered many difficulties but clearly C…B… has
demonstrated enormous strength in making her way in life. Recently R… B… has as
well. That strength and determination is a part of A…B…’s background. These
women have a history and a family experience that belongs to A…B… too.

[
53
]

Ms R…B… has access to
O…B…, A…B…’s brother. If A…B… was placed with her biological family, she could
see her brother.

[
54
]

The Durham CAS plans to
have A…B… adopted by her foster family. The respondent mother and her sister
propose a joint parenting plan that would either grow to parenting by R… B… on
her own or to parenting together or parenting by C… B… on her own. The range of
possibilities depends on the continued improvement and stable parenting by R…
B…. The court has already noted above that the plan of the biological family is
acceptable. It is also clear that A…B… has been well parented in the foster
home. The only caveat about the foster home is Dr. Berman’s hesitancy about
some seeming anxiety in the attachment between A…B… and the foster family as
exhibited by the excessive and peculiar reaction she shows to the access.

[
55
]

If A…B… were to be
asked, no doubt she would prefer her foster family over the unknown of life
with her biological family. However, she is too young to have the cognitive
ability to analyse these options.

[
56
]

Criteria ten speaks to
the effect of delay in the disposition of this case. The delay is shocking and
has had an enormous impact. Not only did A…B… settle into the foster home, but
the access with her mother was so limited that she did not see her mother as a
parent. The mother testified that she was told access would not be increased.
She should have challenged that but her ability to take legal steps was
limited. The agency was not prepared to consider more access as they were
working towards crown wardship with no access so A…B… might be adopted. The
court is concerned that the agency funnelled its energy into their position of
crown wardship, no access, without consideration that there were other
possibilities in this case. Very little effort was expended by the Durham CAS
to help R… B… deal with her problems. While delay lays at the feet of the
agency, the mother and the system, the agency should not make the case for the
parent all the more difficult by limiting the access unless it causes problems
for the child. A…B… had problems with access when it was increased last spring.
This greater access ought to have been routine for her given the mother’s
participation was always diligent and consistent. The agency cannot assume
their claim for crown wardship, no access, is correct before adjudication.
Access should be such as promotes a relationship with a parent unless this
presents difficulties for the child. If there is such a difficulty, a motion
can be brought. The obvious overall solution is that the agency, charged with
the well being of the children in its care, should insist on the timelines in
the Family Law Rules and the
Child and Family Services Act
to ensure the
impact of any disruption is minimized. None of this happened in this case. The
result is that the foster family has experienced a growing commitment to A…B…
resulting in a decision to adopt. This creates anxiety for the foster family
and possibly a transference to A…B…. As well, the biological family has not
been able to see A…B… enough to have a strong connection develop from A…B…’s
perspective.

[
57
]

Criteria eleven directs
the court to consider the harm to A…B… in moving from her foster home and also
in keeping her from her biological family. A…B… does not have a memory of Ms
R…B… as her parent. Her loss in that regard is of connection and of belonging
to her mother and her aunt. At the very least, if R… B… does not continue her
noted life’s improvements, A…B… would have the guidance and control of a quite
impressive woman, C… B…. The progress of these two B… women from their early
sad childhood to what they have achieved is remarkable. A…B… would not know
this if adopted. On the other hand, there is no doubt that A…B… loves her
foster family. They have been her family since she was four months old.

[
58
]

The finding that A…B…
was in need of protection was based on a low level of risk. Quite likely the
risk could have been managed effectively by a placement of A…B… alone with her
mother if proper conditions of supervision could have been worked out. Little
effort was expended on this option.

[
59
]

The paramount purpose
of the
Child and Family Services Act
is the best interest, protection
and well being of children. In reviewing the best interests of A…B… through the
criteria in section 37 (3), the court has found a balance of best interest
between the two options. The court must therefore look to the other purposes in
section 1 (2). They are:

1(2) The additional purposes of this Act, so long as
they are consistent with the best interests, protection and well being of
children are:

1.

To recognize that while
parents may need help in caring for their children, that help should give
support to the autonomy and integrity of the family unit and, wherever
possible, be provided on the basis of mutual consent.

2.

To recognize that the
least disruptive course of action that is available and is appropriate in a
particular case to help a child should be considered.

3.

To recognize that
children’s services should be provided in a manner that,

i.

respects children’s
needs for continuity of care and for stable family relationships, and

ii.

takes in account
physical and mental developmental differences among children.

4.

To recognize that,
wherever possible, services to children and their families should be provided
in a manner that respect cultural, religious and regional differences.

5.

To recognize that
Indian and native people should be entitled to provide, wherever possible,
their own child and family services, and that all services to Indian and native
children and families should be provided in a manner that recognizes their
culture, heritage and traditions and the concept of the extended family.

[
60
]

Criteria four and five
are not applicable in this case. Criteria 1,2 and 3 foreshadow much of the
concerns in section 37(3). The added issue is the emphasis on the autonomy and
integrity of the family unit. This can only be interpreted to be the biological
family.

[
61
]

This court therefore
finds that the intent of the legislation would be to favour the biological
family if all else is equal as in this case.

Order

[
62
]

The court shall order
as follows:

1.

The child A…B… shall be
placed with C… B… and R… B… subject to the supervision of the Children’s Aid
Society of Durham and subject to the following conditions:

1.

Ms. C… B… and Ms. R… B…
shall sign all consents for release of information related to the best
interest, safety and well being of the child.

2.

Ms. C… B… and Ms. R… B…
shall notify the Society at least 30 days prior to any change of address and
phone number.

3.

Ms. C… B… and Ms. R… B…
will permit the Society worker to conduct announced and unannounced home
visits.

4.

Ms. C… B… and Ms. R… B…
will permit the worker to meet with the child at their home; both in their
presence or in private, as requested.

5.

Ms. C… B… and Ms. R… B…
will not permit any babysitters or caregivers or overnight guests to have
contact with the child, without the prior approval of each such person by the
Society, which approval shall be given in writing.

6.

Ms. C… B… and Ms. R… B…
will ensure that the child is not knowingly exposed to any persons that are
involved with prostitution, domestic violence, criminal activity, substance
abuse or any other known child protection concerns as specified in the Child
and Family Services Act.

7.

Ms. C… B… and Ms. R… B…
will ensure that the child has no contact whatsoever with M… C….

8.

Ms. C… B… and Ms. R… B…
shall ensure that the child attends for therapy or counselling as requested by
the Society, and follows through with all recommendations by the therapist or
counsellor. Said therapy or counselling shall be paid for by the Durham
Children’s Aid Society.

9.

Ms. C… B… and Ms. R… B…
will ensure that the child attends medical appointments as required or as
requested and follows through with all recommendations made by the physician.

10.

Each party shall advise the Society forthwith of
any breach of the terms and conditions herein by any other party.

2.

If R… B… breaches any
of the conditions of this order, she shall leave the home of C… B… and C… B…
shall forthwith notify the Durham Children’s Aid Society. The child A…B… shall
then be placed solely in the care and control of C… B… subject to the
supervision of the Durham Children’s Aid Society and the conditions of this
order.

3.

If at any time C… B…
considers the behaviour of R… B… to be unacceptable for continued cohabitation,
C… B… shall notify the Durham Children’s Aid Society and discuss the
difficulties with them. If after the discussion, C… B… considers the continued
cohabitation unacceptable to her, she shall notify R… B… in writing, giving her
twenty-four hours to vacate the premises. The child A…B… shall then be placed
solely in the care and control of C… B….

4.

If R… B… vacates the
home of C… B…, access to A…B… by her mother shall be as agreed between the
Durham Children’s Aid Society, C… B… and R… B….

5.

The Durham Children’s
Aid Society shall provide therapeutic assistance to A… B…, R… B… and C… B… to
assist in the reintegration of A…B… into the household of her mother and her
aunt. If the agency, R… B… and C… B… disagree as to the nature of this
assistance, the agency shall consult with Dr. Berman or a person recommended by
him for direction as to the type of assistance and the frequency of the assistance.
The cost of such consultation and said assistance shall be borne by the Durham
Children’s Aid Society.
